questions.stem: 0.50 mol of sodium chloride is dissolved in water to make 250 mL of solution. What is its concentration?
questions.explanation: c = n ÷ V, with V in litres: 0.50 ÷ 0.250 = 2.0 mol L⁻¹. Dividing by 250 without converting millilitres to litres gives 0.0020, and multiplying instead of dividing gives 0.125 or 125.

questions.stem: A solution contains 5.85 g of sodium chloride in 500 mL. What is its concentration in mol L⁻¹?
questions.explanation: n(NaCl) = 5.85 ÷ 58.5 = 0.100 mol, and c = 0.100 ÷ 0.500 = 0.200 mol L⁻¹. 0.100 is the amount in mol, not the concentration, and 11.7 is the concentration in g L⁻¹.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg sample of bore water contains 0.0060 g of nitrate ions. What is the nitrate concentration in ppm?
questions.explanation: ppm is the mass of solute per million parts by mass of solution, which is the same as mg per kg. 0.0060 g is 6.0 mg, and 6.0 mg ÷ 2.0 kg = 3.0 mg kg⁻¹ = 3.0 ppm. 6.0 ppm forgets to divide by the mass of the sample.

questions.stem: A hand sanitiser is labelled 70% (v/v) ethanol. What does this mean?
options: Every 100 mL of the sanitiser contains 70 mL of ethanol
Every 100 g of the sanitiser contains 70 g of ethanol
Every 100 mL of water has had 70 mL of ethanol added to it
Every 100 mL of the sanitiser contains 70 g of ethanol
questions.explanation: %(v/v) is the volume of solute in every 100 mL of the solution, not of the solvent. Mass in 100 g would be %(m/m), and mass in 100 mL would be %(m/v).

questions.stem: What mass of glucose is needed to make 250 mL of a 5.0% (m/v) glucose solution?
questions.explanation: 5.0% (m/v) means 5.0 g of solute in every 100 mL of solution. For 250 mL, 5.0 × 250 ÷ 100 = 12.5 g. 5.0 g would make only 100 mL of this solution.

questions.stem: A sodium hydroxide solution has a concentration of 0.250 mol L⁻¹. What is its concentration in g L⁻¹?
questions.explanation: M(NaOH) = 23.0 + 16.0 + 1.0 = 40.0 g mol⁻¹, so each litre holds 0.250 × 40.0 = 10.0 g. Dividing the molar mass by the concentration gives 160, and dividing the concentration by the molar mass gives 0.00625.

questions.stem: A dilute solution contains 0.0010 mol L⁻¹ of Cu2+ ions. Taking 1 L of this solution as having a mass of 1 kg, what is the Cu2+ concentration in ppm?
questions.explanation: Each litre holds 0.0010 × 63.5 = 0.0635 g = 63.5 mg of Cu2+. In 1 kg of solution, 63.5 mg kg⁻¹ is 63.5 ppm. 0.0635 is the concentration in g L⁻¹, not mg kg⁻¹.

questions.stem: How does raising the temperature of water generally affect the solubility of a gas such as oxygen in it?
options: Solubility decreases only for gases that react with the water
Solubility decreases, so warm water holds less dissolved oxygen
Solubility increases, so warm water holds more dissolved oxygen
Solubility increases for gases but decreases for all solids
questions.explanation: Gas molecules have more kinetic energy at higher temperatures and escape from solution more easily, so gases become less soluble as water warms. This is why warm water can hold too little oxygen for fish. Most solids become more soluble as temperature rises, not less.

questions.stem: The solubility of potassium nitrate at 40 °C is 64 g per 100 g of water. A solution of 50 g of potassium nitrate in 100 g of water at 40 °C is:
options: unsaturated, because more potassium nitrate could still dissolve
saturated, because it has reached the solubility at this temperature
supersaturated, because the mass dissolved is above the solubility
saturated, because some solid will crystallise out at 40 °C
questions.explanation: A saturated solution holds the maximum amount of solute at that temperature, here 64 g per 100 g of water. With only 50 g dissolved, another 14 g could still dissolve, so the solution is unsaturated and no crystals form.

questions.stem: Potassium nitrate has a solubility of 64 g per 100 g of water at 40 °C and 32 g per 100 g of water at 20 °C. A saturated solution in 200 g of water at 40 °C is cooled to 20 °C. What mass of crystals forms?
questions.explanation: 200 g of water holds 2 × 64 = 128 g at 40 °C but only 2 × 32 = 64 g at 20 °C, so 128 − 64 = 64 g crystallises. 32 g is the answer for only 100 g of water, and 128 g is the total dissolved at 40 °C, not the mass that comes out.

questions.stem: Using the usual solubility rules, which compound is insoluble in water?
questions.explanation: All sodium, potassium and ammonium compounds and all nitrates are soluble. Most sulfates are soluble too, but barium sulfate is one of the exceptions, which is why it is used to detect and measure sulfate ions.

questions.stem: Phosphate ions can be removed from waste water by adding iron(III) chloride. Which ionic equation shows this?
questions.explanation: Iron(III) phosphate is insoluble, so Fe3+ and PO₄3− ions combine in a 1 : 1 ratio, which balances the +3 and −3 charges, and the solid can be settled and filtered out. Fe₃PO₄ would have a charge of +6. Iron(III) chloride is soluble, which is why it can be added as a solution.

questions.stem: Why does adding a suitable precipitating agent remove heavy metal ions such as Pb2+ from water?
options: The ions are changed into a different, non-toxic element
The ions are made more soluble, so they are diluted away
The ions form an insoluble solid that can be settled and filtered out
The ions are changed into a gas that bubbles out of the water
questions.explanation: A precipitating agent supplies anions that form an insoluble compound with the metal ions, such as lead(II) hydroxide or lead(II) sulfide, and the solid is then removed. A chemical reaction cannot change one element into another.

questions.stem: What is a standard solution?
options: A solution made by diluting an acid with distilled water
A solution that changes colour at the equivalence point
A solution whose concentration is accurately known
A solution with a concentration of exactly 1.0 mol L⁻¹
questions.explanation: A standard solution is one whose concentration is known accurately, usually made by dissolving an accurately weighed mass of a pure substance in a volumetric flask. Its concentration can be any value, not only 1.0 mol L⁻¹. A substance that changes colour is an indicator.

questions.stem: Solid sodium hydroxide is not used to make a standard solution by weighing. Why?
options: Its molar mass is too large for small amounts of it to be weighed accurately
It reacts too slowly with acids for a sharp end point to be seen in a titration
It absorbs water and carbon dioxide from the air, so its measured mass is not reliable
It is a strong base that ionises completely, so its solutions are too concentrated
questions.explanation: To make a standard solution the mass weighed must be all the pure compound. Sodium hydroxide takes up water and reacts with CO₂ from the air, so a weighed sample is not pure NaOH. Its molar mass, 40.0 g mol⁻¹, is small, and it reacts rapidly with acids.

questions.stem: What volume of 2.00 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid is needed to make 500 mL of 0.100 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid?
questions.explanation: The amount of HCl does not change on dilution, so c₁V₁ = c₂V₂: V₁ = 0.100 × 500 ÷ 2.00 = 25.0 mL. That 25.0 mL is made up to 500 mL with water in a volumetric flask.

questions.stem: A 25.00 mL aliquot of sodium hydroxide solution is titrated with 0.100 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid. The average titre is 20.00 mL. What is the concentration of the sodium hydroxide?
questions.explanation: n(HCl) = 0.100 × 0.02000 = 0.00200 mol, and the ratio is 1 : 1, so n(NaOH) = 0.00200 mol. c(NaOH) = 0.00200 ÷ 0.02500 = 0.0800 mol L⁻¹. 0.125 comes from swapping the two volumes.

questions.stem: A 20.00 mL aliquot of sulfuric acid is titrated with 0.150 mol L⁻¹ sodium hydroxide, and the titre is 24.00 mL. What is the concentration of the sulfuric acid?
questions.explanation: n(NaOH) = 0.150 × 0.02400 = 0.00360 mol. From H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O, n(H₂SO₄) = 0.00360 ÷ 2 = 0.00180 mol, so c = 0.00180 ÷ 0.02000 = 0.0900 mol L⁻¹. 0.180 forgets that sulfuric acid is diprotic.

questions.stem: 10.00 mL of vinegar was diluted to 100.0 mL. A 25.00 mL aliquot of the diluted solution needed 21.00 mL of 0.100 mol L⁻¹ NaOH. What is the ethanoic acid concentration of the original vinegar?
questions.explanation: n(NaOH) = 0.100 × 0.02100 = 0.00210 mol = n(CH₃COOH) in the aliquot, so the diluted solution is 0.00210 ÷ 0.02500 = 0.0840 mol L⁻¹. The vinegar was diluted tenfold, so the original is 0.840 mol L⁻¹. 0.0840 is the diluted concentration.

questions.stem: Before a titration, the burette should be rinsed with:
options: distilled water only, and then filled while it is still wet
a small volume of the solution that is in the conical flask
ethanol, so that it dries quickly before it is filled
a small volume of the solution it is about to be filled with
questions.explanation: Rinsing with the solution it will deliver removes water and other residues that would dilute that solution and change its concentration. Leaving the burette wet with distilled water would dilute the titrant, so a larger titre would be needed.

questions.stem: Why is an indicator added to the conical flask in an acid-base titration?
options: It neutralises any excess acid or base left over at the end of the titration
It makes the solution conduct, so the end point can be detected by a meter
Its colour change shows the end point, which should match the equivalence point
It speeds up the reaction between the acid and the base in the flask
questions.explanation: An indicator is a weak acid or base whose two forms have different colours, so it changes colour over a small pH range. A suitable indicator changes colour, at the end point, very close to the equivalence point, when the reactants are in their mole ratio. It is used in tiny amounts and is not a catalyst.

questions.stem: A student rinsed the pipette with distilled water before using it to deliver the aliquot of acid being analysed. How will this affect the calculated concentration of the acid?
options: It will be too low, because the water reacts with some of the acid in the aliquot
It will be too low, because the diluted aliquot contained fewer moles of acid
It will be too high, because the extra water in the aliquot adds to its volume
It will be unchanged, because water does not react with the base in the burette
questions.explanation: Water left in the pipette dilutes the acid, so the 20.00 mL or 25.00 mL delivered contains less acid than it should. A smaller titre is needed, and the calculation, which assumes the full aliquot volume of undiluted acid, gives a concentration that is too low. The water does not react; it simply dilutes.

questions.stem: CO₂, CH₄ and H₂O contribute to the greenhouse effect because they:
options: react with oxygen and release heat into the air
absorb infrared radiation emitted by Earth's surface
absorb ultraviolet radiation and break down ozone
reflect visible sunlight back towards space
questions.explanation: Earth's surface emits infrared radiation, and these gases absorb it and re-emit it in all directions, including back towards the surface, which warms the lower atmosphere. Reflecting sunlight to space would cool Earth, and ozone breakdown is a separate issue involving ultraviolet light.

questions.stem: What is the enhanced greenhouse effect?
options: The natural warming of Earth by water vapour alone, without any carbon dioxide
The cooling of Earth that happens when greenhouse gas levels fall below normal
The extra warming caused by human-driven increases in greenhouse gas concentrations
The warming caused by gases that absorb ultraviolet radiation in the upper atmosphere
questions.explanation: The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm enough for life. Human activities such as burning fossil fuels and agriculture have raised the concentrations of CO₂ and CH₄, so more infrared radiation is absorbed and extra warming results. Greenhouse gases act by absorbing infrared, not ultraviolet, radiation.

questions.stem: What are standard laboratory conditions (SLC)?
questions.explanation: SLC are 25 °C (298 K) and 100 kPa, and under these conditions one mole of any gas occupies 24.8 L. 101.3 kPa is one atmosphere, which is not part of the definition of SLC.

questions.stem: Gas pressure is caused by:
options: the weight of the container pressing down on the gas
gas particles reacting chemically with the container walls
gas particles colliding with the walls of their container
gas particles attracting each other strongly as they move
questions.explanation: Pressure is force per unit area. Gas particles move rapidly and randomly and exert a force each time they strike a surface, so more frequent or more energetic collisions mean higher pressure. Attractions between gas particles are very weak.

questions.stem: A gas has a pressure of 1.50 atm. What is this pressure in kPa?
questions.explanation: 1 atm = 101.3 kPa, so 1.50 × 101.3 = 152 kPa. 150 kPa wrongly takes 1 atm as 100 kPa, and 67.5 kPa divides instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: What amount of gas occupies 2.00 L at 100 kPa and 27 °C?
questions.explanation: n = pV ÷ RT, with T = 27 + 273 = 300 K: n = (100 × 2.00) ÷ (8.31 × 300) = 200 ÷ 2493 = 0.0802 mol. Using 27 instead of 300 K gives 0.891 mol, and using pressure in Pa with volume in L gives 80.2 mol.

questions.stem: What volume does 0.500 mol of nitrogen gas occupy at 200 kPa and 127 °C?
questions.explanation: V = nRT ÷ p, with T = 127 + 273 = 400 K: V = (0.500 × 8.31 × 400) ÷ 200 = 8.31 L. Using 127 instead of 400 K gives 2.64 L, and 8310 confuses litres with millilitres.

questions.stem: Calcium carbonate reacts with excess hydrochloric acid: CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). What volume of CO₂ at SLC is produced from 0.200 mol of CaCO₃?
questions.explanation: The mole ratio CaCO₃ : CO₂ is 1 : 1, so 0.200 mol of CO₂ forms, and V = n × Vm = 0.200 × 24.8 = 4.96 L. 9.92 L wrongly uses the 2 from the HCl, and 24.8 L is the volume of one whole mole.

questions.stem: Magnesium reacts with excess hydrochloric acid: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g). What mass of magnesium produces 2.48 L of hydrogen gas at SLC?
questions.explanation: n(H₂) = 2.48 ÷ 24.8 = 0.100 mol. The ratio Mg : H₂ is 1 : 1, so n(Mg) = 0.100 mol and m = 0.100 × 24.3 = 2.43 g. 4.86 g doubles the amount using the coefficient of HCl, and 60.3 g multiplies the volume by the molar mass.

questions.stem: Methane burns according to CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g). What volume of oxygen is needed to burn 5.0 L of methane, with both gases at the same temperature and pressure?
questions.explanation: At the same temperature and pressure, equal volumes of gases contain equal amounts in mol, so volumes react in the same ratio as the coefficients. Two volumes of oxygen are needed for each volume of methane: 2 × 5.0 = 10 L. 2.5 L inverts the ratio.

questions.stem: A reaction produced 0.00400 mol of gas, which occupied 99.2 mL at SLC. What molar volume does this result give?
questions.explanation: Molar volume = V ÷ n = 0.0992 L ÷ 0.00400 mol = 24.8 L mol⁻¹, which agrees with the value at SLC. Leaving the volume in millilitres gives 24 800, and dividing n by V gives 0.0403.

questions.stem: A 0.640 g sample of an unknown gas occupies 496 mL at SLC. What is its molar mass?
questions.explanation: n = 0.496 ÷ 24.8 = 0.0200 mol, and M = m ÷ n = 0.640 ÷ 0.0200 = 32.0 g mol⁻¹, which fits oxygen gas, O₂. 0.0313 comes from dividing the amount by the mass, and 16.0 is half the correct value.

questions.stem: Why can electrical conductivity be used to estimate the salinity of a water sample?
options: Dissolved salts release ions, and more ions make the water conduct better
Salt molecules carry delocalised electrons that move through the water
Pure water conducts strongly, and dissolved salt reduces how well it conducts
Dissolved salt lowers the pH, and the conductivity meter detects the pH
questions.explanation: Salts dissociate into ions in water, and these mobile ions carry the current, so conductivity rises with the concentration of dissolved salts. Pure water conducts very poorly. Ionic compounds release ions, not delocalised electrons, and a conductivity meter does not measure pH.

questions.stem: Which is a likely source of heavy metal ions, such as lead and cadmium, in soil or water?
options: Carbon dioxide dissolving from the air
Leaves decomposing on the forest floor
Rain falling on clean quartz sand
Run-off from mine sites and industrial waste
questions.explanation: Heavy metals are released when ores are mined and processed and when industrial wastes are discharged, and they can then leach into soil and waterways. Carbon dioxide and decomposing leaves contain no heavy metals, and quartz is silicon dioxide.

questions.stem: A 2.50 g sample of hydrated copper(II) sulfate, CuSO₄.xH₂O, is heated to constant mass, leaving 1.60 g of anhydrous CuSO₄. What is the value of x?
questions.explanation: Mass of water lost = 2.50 − 1.60 = 0.90 g, so n(H₂O) = 0.90 ÷ 18.0 = 0.050 mol. n(CuSO₄) = 1.60 ÷ 159.6 = 0.0100 mol, and 0.050 ÷ 0.0100 = 5, so the formula is CuSO₄.5H₂O. Using the hydrated mass, 2.50 g, as if it were all CuSO₄ gives about 3.

questions.stem: When finding the water of hydration of a salt, why is the sample heated to constant mass?
options: To let the sample cool evenly before it is weighed each time
To make sure all of the water of crystallisation has been driven off
To make the salt react with oxygen so that its mass increases
To decompose the salt completely into the elements it contains
questions.explanation: Each heating drives off more water, so the mass keeps falling until no water is left. Two equal masses in a row show that all the water has gone, so the mass lost is all water. If water remained, x would come out too small.

questions.stem: Excess silver nitrate solution is added to a solution containing 0.0500 mol of sodium chloride. What mass of silver chloride precipitates?
questions.explanation: Ag+(aq) + Cl−(aq) → AgCl(s), so 0.0500 mol of chloride gives 0.0500 mol of AgCl. M(AgCl) = 107.9 + 35.5 = 143.4 g mol⁻¹, and 0.0500 × 143.4 = 7.17 g. 2.93 g is the mass of the sodium chloride, not the precipitate.

questions.stem: The sulfate in a 50.0 mL water sample is precipitated as barium sulfate, and 0.233 g of dry BaSO₄ is collected. What was the sulfate concentration in mol L⁻¹?
questions.explanation: M(BaSO₄) = 137.3 + 32.1 + 4 × 16.0 = 233.4 g mol⁻¹, so n = 0.233 ÷ 233.4 = 0.00100 mol, which is also the amount of sulfate. c = 0.00100 ÷ 0.0500 = 0.0200 mol L⁻¹. 0.00100 is the amount in mol, and 0.0485 uses the molar mass of sulfate instead of barium sulfate.

questions.stem: Calcium carbonate decomposes on heating: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g). What mass of carbon dioxide is produced from 10.0 g of calcium carbonate?
questions.explanation: M(CaCO₃) = 40.1 + 12.0 + 48.0 = 100.1 g mol⁻¹, so n = 10.0 ÷ 100.1 = 0.0999 mol. One mol of CO₂ forms per mol of CaCO₃, so m = 0.0999 × 44.0 = 4.40 g. 5.60 g is the mass of calcium oxide left behind.

questions.stem: In colorimetry, why is a calibration curve prepared?
options: To remove any impurities from the unknown sample before it is measured
To relate absorbance to concentration using standards of known concentration
To find the wavelength at which the solvent itself absorbs most strongly
To compare the colour of the unknown sample with the standards by eye
questions.explanation: Standards of known concentration are measured and their absorbances plotted against concentration. The unknown's absorbance is then read off this line to find its concentration. The instrument measures absorbance, so no judgement of colour by eye is needed.

questions.stem: Iron standards of 0, 2.0, 4.0 and 6.0 mg L⁻¹ gave absorbances of 0.00, 0.15, 0.30 and 0.45. A water sample, treated in the same way, had an absorbance of 0.24. What is its iron concentration?
questions.explanation: The absorbance rises by 0.075 for each 1.0 mg L⁻¹, so 0.24 ÷ 0.075 = 3.2 mg L⁻¹. This lies between the 2.0 and 4.0 mg L⁻¹ standards, as its absorbance lies between 0.15 and 0.30.

questions.stem: The absorbance of a sample is higher than that of the most concentrated standard on the calibration curve. What should the analyst do?
options: Report the concentration of the most concentrated standard as the result
Dilute the sample by a known factor so that its absorbance falls within the standards
Extend the calibration line beyond the standards and read the concentration from it
Change to a wavelength at which the coloured species absorbs more strongly
questions.explanation: A calibration curve is reliable only over the range of the standards, and the relationship may not stay linear beyond it. Diluting by a known factor brings the absorbance into range, and the result is multiplied by that factor. A wavelength of stronger absorption would raise the absorbance further.

questions.stem: In UV-visible spectroscopy, why is the analysis done at the wavelength that the coloured species absorbs most strongly?
options: It is the wavelength that the solution transmits most, so the detector reads it easily
It is the colour that the solution appears to the eye, so it matches the visible colour
At that wavelength the absorbance stays the same whatever the concentration
Absorbance changes most with concentration there, so the measurement is most sensitive
questions.explanation: At the absorption maximum each change in concentration gives the largest change in absorbance, so small differences can be detected. A solution appears the colour it transmits, which is roughly the complement of the colour it absorbs most.
